title: 3-Read Friday #1: Pre-Observation Coaching, Consistency, and Worked Examples
author: Barton, Craig
summary: In the inaugural issue of his 3-Read Friday newsletter, Craig Barton shares three blog posts he found valuable that week and adds his own short editorial gloss on each. He first highlights Ollie Lovell's suggestions for structuring the pre-observation conversation in instructional coaching, tying it to his own work coaching maths teachers and admitting he still has room to grow as a coach. He then turns to Chris Such's "The Cost of Consistency," which pushes back on Barton's own instinct that trading teacher autonomy for department-wide consistency is usually worth it. He closes with Alex Blanksby's "Five Ways to Use Worked Examples," which Barton connects to his own Silent Teacher approach and to ideas about sequencing maximally different positive examples. Across the three items, coaching practice and curriculum consistency dominate over the pedagogy-of-worked-examples item, so the issue centers on the practice-and-culture side of teaching rather than instructional technique alone.
points: Barton frames the pre-observation conversation itself, not just the post-lesson feedback, as the coach's real lever for a productive outcome, per Lovell's framing.
He flags his own bias toward trading teacher autonomy for departmental consistency, and credits Such's post with complicating that view.
He connects Blanksby's worked-examples advice directly to his own Silent Teacher method, showing how he filters new reading through existing practice.
quotes: Ollie offers three super useful suggestions for the conversation that coaches - or anyone who observes a colleague’s lesson - can have before the feedback session to increase the chance of a positive, productive outcome.
I am always interested in the level of autonomy teachers have in the classroom.
In many of the maths departments I support, I feel less autonomy is a price worth paying for greater consistency - for example, insisting staff use certain high-quality resources or approaches.
Chris Such has made me consider a different side to this argument.

I found this post super useful for ideas I can build into my current practice (I initially deliver worked examples in silence using my Silent Teacher approach), but also for ideas about alternate ways to deliver worked examples, such as presenting completed solutions and using maximally different positive examples.
